objective_text: Construct truth tables for compound propositions

questions.stem: Create a truth table for the proposition (P ∧ Q) → R.
questions.solution:
The truth table for (P ∧ Q) → R is as follows:

P  | Q  |  (P ∧ Q)  |  (P ∧ Q) → R
---|---|---------|----------------
T   | T  |   T     |      T          
T   | F  |   F     |      F          
F   | T  |   F     |      T          
F   | F  |   F     |      T          

So the correct answer is [T, T, F, F].
questions.explanation: This truth table shows that (P ∧ Q) → R is true when (P ∧ Q) is false or R is true.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to assume that (P ∧ Q) → R is always true, which is incorrect. It's only true when the antecedent (P ∧ Q) is false or the consequent (R) is true.

questions.stem: Construct a truth table for the proposition P ↔ (Q ∨ ¬S).

choices.A: [T, T, F, T],  [F, F, T, F]
choices.B: [T, F, T, F],  [F, T, F, T]
choices.C: [T, T, F, F],  [F, F, T, T]
choices.D: [T, F, T, T],  [F, T, F, F]

questions.solution:
The truth table for P ↔ (Q ∨ ¬S) is as follows:

P  | Q  | S  | Q ∨ ¬S  | P ↔ (Q ∨ ¬S)
---|---|---|--------|----------------
T   | T  | T  |   T     |      F          
T   | T  | F  |   T     |      T          
T   | F  | T  |   T     |      T          
T   | F  | F  |   F     |      F          
F   | T  | T  |   T     |      T          
F   | T  | F  |   T     |      F          
F   | F  | T  |   F     |      T          
F   | F  | F  |   F     |      T          

So the correct answer is [T, F, T, F],  [F, T, F, T].
questions.explanation: This truth table shows that P ↔ (Q ∨ ¬S) is true when P and (Q ∨ ¬S) have the same truth value.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to mix up the order of the biconditional operator, which would result in a different truth table. Remember that P ↔ Q is equivalent to (P → Q) ∧ (Q → P).

questions.stem: Write a truth table for the proposition (¬P ∨ Q) ∧  (R ∨ S).

choices.A: [T, T, T, F],  [T, F, T, F],  [F, T, T, T],  [F, F, T, T]
choices.B: [T, T, T, T],  [T, F, T, T],  [F, T, T, F],  [F, F, T, F]
choices.C: [T, T, F, T],  [T, F, F, T],  [F, T, F, F],  [F, F, F, F]
choices.D: [T, T, T, F],  [T, F, T, F],  [F, T, T, F],  [F, F, T, F]

questions.solution:
The truth table for (¬P ∨ Q) ∧  (R ∨ S) is as follows:

P  | Q  | R  | S  | ¬P ∨ Q  | R ∨ S  |  (¬P ∨ Q) ∧  (R ∨ S)
---|---|---|---|---------|--------|----------------------
T   | T  | T  | T  |    F     |   T     |        F              
T   | F  | T  | T  |    T     |   T     |        T              
F   | T  | T  | T  |    T     |   T     |        T              
F   | F  | T  | T  |    T     |   T     |        T              
T   | T  | F  | T  |    F     |   T     |        F              
T   | F  | F  | T  |    T     |   T     |        T              
F   | T  | F  | T  |    T     |   T     |        T              
F   | F  | F  | T  |    T     |   T     |        T              

So the correct answer is [T, T, T, F],  [T, F, T, F],  [F, T, T, T],  [F, F, T, T].
questions.explanation: This truth table shows that (¬P ∨ Q) ∧  (R ∨ S) is true when both (¬P ∨ Q) and (R ∨ S) are true.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to forget to apply the distributive law, which would result in an incorrect truth table. Remember that (A ∧ B) ∨ C is equivalent to (A ∨ C) ∧ (B ∨ C).

questions.stem: Create a truth table for the proposition (P → Q) ↔  (¬Q → ¬P).
questions.solution:
The truth table for (P → Q) ↔  (¬Q → ¬P) is as follows:

P  | Q  | P → Q  | ¬Q  | ¬Q → ¬P  |  (P → Q) ↔  (¬Q → ¬P)
---|---|-------|----|---------|------------------------
T   | T  |   T    | F   |    T     |        T                
T   | F  |   F    | T   |    T     |        F                
F   | T  |   T    | F   |    T     |        T                
F   | F  |   T    | T   |    T     |        T                

So the correct answer is [T, T, F],  [F, F, T].
questions.explanation: This truth table shows that (P → Q) ↔  (¬Q → ¬P) is true when both conditional statements have the same truth value.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to assume that (P → Q) ↔  (¬Q → ¬P) is always true, which is incorrect. It's only true when P and Q are logically equivalent.

questions.stem: Construct a truth table for the proposition (P ∧ R) ∨  (Q ∧ ¬R).

choices.A: [T, T, T, F],  [T, F, T, F],  [F, T, T, T],  [F, F, T, T]
choices.B: [T, T, T, T],  [T, F, T, T],  [F, T, T, F],  [F, F, T, F]
choices.C: [T, T, F, T],  [T, F, F, T],  [F, T, F, F],  [F, F, F, F]
choices.D: [T, T, T, F],  [T, F, T, F],  [F, T, T, F],  [F, F, T, F]

questions.solution:
The truth table for (P ∧ R) ∨  (Q ∧ ¬R) is as follows:

P  | R  | Q  | ¬R  | P ∧ R  | Q ∧ ¬R  |  (P ∧ R) ∨  (Q ∧ ¬R)
---|---|---|----|-------|---------|----------------------
T   | T  | T  | F   |   T    |    F     |        T              
T   | F  | T  | T   |   F    |    T     |        T              
F   | T  | T  | F   |   F    |    F     |        F              
F   | F  | T  | T   |   F    |    T     |        T              

So the correct answer is [T, T, T, F],  [T, F, T, F],  [F, T, T, T],  [F, F, T, T].
questions.explanation: This truth table shows that (P ∧ R) ∨  (Q ∧ ¬R) is true when either (P ∧ R) or (Q ∧ ¬R) is true.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to forget to apply the distributive law, which would result in an incorrect truth table. Remember that A ∨ (B ∧ C) is equivalent to (A ∨ B) ∧ (A ∨ C).

questions.stem: Write a truth table for the proposition P →  (Q ∨ R) ↔  (¬P ∨ Q) ∧  (¬P ∨ R).
questions.explanation: This truth table shows that P →  (Q ∨ R) ↔  (¬P ∨ Q) ∧  (¬P ∨ R) is true when both conditional statements have the same truth value.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to assume that P →  (Q ∨ R) ↔  (¬P ∨ Q) ∧  (¬P ∨ R) is always true, which is incorrect. It's only true when P and (Q ∨ R) are logically equivalent.

questions.stem: Construct a truth table for the proposition (P ∨ Q) → R ↔  (¬R → ¬P) ∧  (¬R → ¬Q).
questions.explanation: This truth table shows that (P ∨ Q) → R ↔  (¬R → ¬P) ∧  (¬R → ¬Q) is true when both conditional statements have the same truth value.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to assume that (P ∨ Q) → R ↔  (¬R → ¬P) ∧  (¬R → ¬Q) is always true, which is incorrect. It's only true when P ∨ Q and R are logically equivalent.
